title: Databases
lesson: A database keeps records and gives callers rules for reading and changing them. Start a design by listing the queries, relationships, and updates that must succeed together.
example: A train reservation must claim a seat and record the booking together. A transaction adds coordination but prevents a half-booked seat.
question: Which requirement matters most when choosing storage for a seat reservation?
answers: Whether related changes can commit atomically
Whether the engine stores timestamps as text
Whether every table fits in memory
why: A failed booking should leave the seat and reservation records in agreement.
detail: Follow a $20 bank transfer through ACID. Atomicity commits the debit and credit together. Consistency preserves declared rules, such as a valid account reference on each entry. Isolation controls what concurrent transfers can see or change. Durability preserves the acknowledged transfer through the failures covered by the storage contract. Keeping the two amounts equal still requires correct transaction logic or an enforced constraint. A database cannot infer that rule from two numbers.

terms.definition: Atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability describe different properties of a transaction.
A rule that must remain true across successful changes, such as a ledger's entries balancing.
The decision to accept a transaction's changes as a unit.

references.title: Scaling up to your first 10 million users

story.intro: Two people tap the last window seat on the same train. Whose ticket is valid?
story.meaning: A database keeps records and can enforce rules about which changes are allowed together.

steps.label: Claim seat 12A
steps.caption: Mina's request asks the database to claim seat 12A and create her ticket together.

steps.label: Commit booking
steps.caption: Both changes succeed. The database keeps the booking even after the app restarts.

steps.label: Try seat 12A
steps.caption: Leo's request arrives for the same train and seat. A rule allowing only one booking rejects it.

story.technology: In PostgreSQL, a transaction groups the changes, and a unique constraint can protect each train-and-seat pair.

title: SQL vs NoSQL
lesson: Relational systems model rows, constraints, and joins. Nonrelational systems offer models such as documents, graphs, and key-value pairs. Compare the particular engine's transaction, query, and scaling behavior against your workload.
example: A meal-kit service joins orders, refunds, and customers for changing reports. A relational model supports new joins, while a document model can make one known order view cheap.
question: Analysts often invent new joins across orders and refunds. Which capability deserves priority?
answers: Flexible relational queries
Maximum single-key write speed
Document nesting depth
why: Unplanned combinations of related records favor a query engine that can join them directly.
detail: Ask two separate questions. How will a page find its records, and which updates must be observed together? SQL tables can serve stale reads from asynchronous replicas. Some document stores support multi-document ACID transactions, even across shards. Compare a concrete operation, such as reserving inventory and recording an order, under each engine's configured isolation, read location, and acknowledgment policy. Transaction coordination can add latency across machines.

terms.definition: Atomicity commits all the steps together. Consistency preserves the rules a transaction must obey. Isolation governs how concurrent transactions interact. Durability keeps committed changes through the failures the database promises to tolerate.

Basically available means useful service can continue during a failure. Soft state means background updates can change what a reader sees. Eventually consistent means replicas can converge once writes stop and communication recovers.
The set of records, partitions, or databases one transaction can update together.

references.title: Types of NoSQL Databases: How to Choose the Right One
SQL vs. NoSQL Databases: What’s the Difference?

story.intro: A shop needs yesterday’s sales by supplier and a one-tap view of a saved cart. Which records does each screen need?
story.meaning: If the shop keeps sales and suppliers in separate tables, a SQL query can match them up. A document database can keep a whole cart in one record. Start with what the screen needs to show.

steps.label: Match supplier IDs
steps.caption: Each item names its supplier. Joining the records lets the report total sales by supplier.

steps.label: Look up cart
steps.caption: The screen already knows the cart ID. One document can hold the small list of items it needs.

steps.label: Check purchase rules
steps.caption: Now ask whether charging credit and reducing stock must succeed together. Inspect the selected engine's transaction guarantees.

story.technology: PostgreSQL supports joins across tables, and MongoDB can store a cart document and also supports multi-document transactions.

title: Replication
lesson: Replication keeps copies of the same records on multiple nodes. A follower that applies writes asynchronously can trail the primary, even when both machines are healthy.
example: Sending catalog reads to replicas reduces primary load. A shopper who just edited an item may need to read from the primary to see the change immediately.
question: An edit succeeds but a follower shows the old title. What explains it?
answers: The follower has yet to apply the write
The row was split across two shards
The index cannot store changed text
why: A write can be acknowledged before asynchronous replicas receive and apply it.
detail: Suppose the leader acknowledges version 19 while a nearby follower still serves version 18. A client can carry the acknowledged version into its next request. The service then picks a replica that has applied at least version 19, waits briefly, or reads from the leader. That makes a profile edit visible to its author while allowing other readers to use slightly stale copies.

terms.definition: The distance in time or log position between the primary and a replica.
A session guarantee that a reader can observe its own completed writes or newer values.
An ordered record of changes a follower can replay.

references.title: Database Replication Introduction: Types and Advantages

story.intro: Jin updates their display name. Their profile saves, but the nearby server still shows the old name.
story.meaning: Replication copies stored changes between servers. A copy updated in the background can briefly lag behind the original.

steps.label: Save new name
steps.caption: The primary records Jin's new name and confirms the save.

steps.label: Serve old name
steps.caption: A read reaches the copy before the change arrives. It still returns the old name.

steps.label: Send name change
steps.caption: The copy applies the change. Later reads there can see the new name too.

story.technology: With a PostgreSQL read replica, the app can read from the primary immediately after a profile edit.

title: Sharding
lesson: Sharding divides records across machines using a partition key. The key determines both the spread of writes and how many shards a query must visit.
example: Partitioning messages by conversation keeps a chat history together. One viral conversation can still overload its shard.
question: All writes for a celebrity's chat land on one server. What is the likely cause?
answers: A hot partition key
Slow replication across every shard
A missing join index on author names
why: A shard can become saturated when one value receives a disproportionate share of the traffic.
detail: Hashing a customer ID spreads distinct customers among buckets. A query for one customer can route directly, while a query for all customers in a city may contact every bucket. Range partitioning can make ordered scans cheaper, but sequential timestamps can direct all new writes to the newest range. Estimate both how many keys exist and how traffic is distributed across them before choosing.

terms.definition: The value or combination of values used to choose a record's shard.
Sending a query to multiple shards and combining the replies.
Moving partitions between nodes as load or capacity changes.

story.intro: A library keeps millions of book records. Its catalogue is outgrowing one database. How can it split the work and still find a book?
story.meaning: Sharding means dividing records between databases. Each database holds a slice called a shard. A rule tells the app which slice to use for each record.

steps.label: Book 42
steps.caption: The app wants book 42. In this small example, even book numbers belong on one shard and odd numbers on the other.

steps.label: Even number
steps.caption: 42 is even. The app can ask Shard A directly, without searching both databases.

steps.label: Odd number
steps.caption: For book 43, the app asks Shard B. A search by author is harder because one author’s books can be on both shards.

story.technology: MongoDB uses a shard key to decide where documents belong. A book number is one possible key; the even-or-odd rule here illustrates splitting records.

title: Federation
lesson: Federation divides storage by business function, with different databases owning different kinds of records. Work confined to one domain can scale independently, while cross-domain reports need explicit integration.
example: Moving billing and inventory to separate databases isolates billing traffic. A report matching invoices to warehouse shipments now has to combine data across systems.
question: Which split is federation by function?
answers: Orders in one database and fulfillment in another
Even order IDs on one node and odd IDs on another
An identical orders table copied to three nodes
why: Each database owns a different domain of data.
detail: Start from a question about ownership. If billing corrects an invoice, inventory should learn only about events it needs. A report joining both domains can consume changes into a separate reporting store. The fields can briefly describe different moments if one feed falls behind. Publish the update time or reconcile a common checkpoint when a report needs a consistent cutoff.

terms.definition: A division around a business responsibility with a clear owner for its records.
A stream describing inserts, updates, and deletes for downstream consumers.

story.intro: Payroll runs a report while warehouse staff scan deliveries. These two parts of the business work with different records.
story.meaning: Federation separates databases by responsibility. Each owns one kind of data and can handle its own workload.

steps.label: Save payslip
steps.caption: The pay run writes employee payment records to its own database.

steps.label: Save delivery
steps.caption: Scanning a pallet updates stock in a separate database. That database handles warehouse traffic.

steps.label: Combine summaries
steps.caption: A cost report needs wages and stock totals, so a reporting job assembles summaries from both owners.

story.technology: Two PostgreSQL databases can hold the payroll and stock records, with a reporting job reading agreed exports.

title: Denormalization
lesson: Denormalization copies or precomputes data so common reads need fewer joins. Every duplicate creates a maintenance decision when the original changes.
example: A feed card stores the author's display name alongside its post. Reading a page is cheap, but a rename may take time to reach old cards.
question: A team copies author names into feed rows. Which cost should it design for?
answers: Keeping copied names in sync after edits
Routing every read through a cross-table join
Losing the ability to index post IDs
why: One edit to the original may require changes to many stored copies.
detail: Decide whether a copied field represents a historical snapshot or the latest value. An invoice usually keeps the delivery address used at purchase, even after the customer moves. A public profile name on an old comment may need to follow later edits. For a live copy, identify the authoritative record, propagate changes, and provide a way to repair missed updates.

terms.definition: The authoritative record used to resolve disagreements between copies.
The extra writes incurred when one logical change updates several stored records.

story.intro: Nora’s news feed shows an author name on every post. Reading 30 posts could mean asking for 30 names.
story.meaning: Denormalization stores a useful extra copy to make a common read cheaper. You must decide what happens when the original changes.

steps.label: Copy display name
steps.caption: At publication, the app saves the author's display name beside the post.

steps.label: Read post cards
steps.caption: The feed can now get text and names in one read.

steps.label: Refresh old names
steps.caption: If posts should show the current name, the app must update those copies after a rename.

story.technology: A PostgreSQL post row can store both an author ID and a copied display name for a busy feed.

title: SQL Tuning
lesson: Find a slow query under representative load and inspect its execution plan. Compare row counts, scans, sorts, and joins before changing indexes or rewriting SQL.
example: A lookup reads millions of orders to find six for one customer. An index on the customer key can reduce reads, at the cost of extra work on writes.
question: A slow query returns six rows. Which evidence best guides an index decision?
answers: The query plan and rows scanned
The maximum length of table names
The total number of application routes
why: The plan shows how the engine locates rows and where it spends work.
detail: Compare estimated and actual rows near the first expensive step. An estimate of ten matches that becomes 500,000 can cause an expensive nested-loop join. Outdated statistics, correlated columns, or a filter unsuitable for the index can explain the gap. Test a change with representative parameters. A table scan can be cheaper when the query returns most of the table.

terms.definition: The engine's chosen sequence of scans, joins, sorts, and other operations.
How much of a table a condition matches. A highly selective condition returns few rows.
Summaries of data distribution that help the planner estimate costs.

story.intro: A library search takes two seconds to find three books by ISBN. Where is the time going?
story.meaning: SQL tuning means measuring how the database runs a query and changing the work it does.

steps.label: Inspect plan
steps.caption: The plan shows the engine checked every shelf record to find three matches.

steps.label: Index ISBN
steps.caption: An index builds a lookup path from ISBN to matching rows. New books now need an index update too.

steps.label: Measure again
steps.caption: Run the same lookup with realistic data. Compare rows examined and time before keeping the change.

story.technology: PostgreSQL's EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports what a query actually did when it ran.

title: RDBMS
lesson: A relational database management system stores data in related tables. Keys identify rows, constraints enforce rules, and transactions group changes into one commit.
example: A school links enrollments to existing students using a foreign key. The check costs a little on writes and prevents orphan records.
question: Which database feature rejects an enrollment for a nonexistent student?
answers: A foreign key constraint
A read replica
A covering index
why: The constraint requires a matching key in the referenced student table.
detail: Concurrent correctness matters even when each request succeeds on its own. Two customers can read the last seat as available before either books it. A unique constraint on the seat and departure can reject the second booking. More complex rules may need locks or serializable transactions. Applications using serializable isolation must be ready to retry a transaction that conflicts with another.

terms.definition: A unique, non-null identifier for each row in a table.
Committed transactions have an outcome equivalent to executing them one at a time in some order.
An engine-enforced rule preventing duplicate key values under the database's uniqueness semantics.

references.title: SQL vs. NoSQL Databases: What’s the Difference?

story.intro: A school sees an enrollment for student 77, but there is no student 77. How can the store reject that mistake?
story.meaning: A relational database management system keeps linked tables and checks rules such as which student an enrollment can reference.

steps.label: Create student
steps.caption: The school registers student 25. The table gives that student a unique ID.

steps.label: Reference student 25
steps.caption: The new enrollment names an existing student, so the database accepts it.

steps.label: Reference student 77
steps.caption: A foreign key requires a matching student row. The second request fails before an orphan enrollment can appear.

story.technology: A PostgreSQL foreign key can connect the student ID in enrollments to the primary key in students.

title: Key-Value Store
lesson: A key-value store retrieves or replaces a value using its key. Lookups are simple when the caller knows that key, while searching inside values may require another structure.
example: A session ID looks up one session record efficiently. Listing sessions by city requires an index or a different access path.
question: Which workload fits basic key-value access?
answers: Load a session by its opaque session ID
Follow a chain of referrals across accounts
Group all purchases by daily profit
why: Each session read already has the exact key needed to locate the value.
detail: Think through an update as well as a lookup. Two workers read stock level 8, each subtracts 1, and both write 7. A conditional update compares the stored version with the version previously read. The second worker then retries against fresh state. An atomic decrement supported by the store can also express this operation without a read-modify-write race.

terms.definition: Change a value only when its current version or value matches an expected one.
One writer overwrites another writer's change after both read the same earlier state.

story.intro: A visitor returns with session ID k42. The app needs just the saved session for that ID.
story.meaning: A key-value store associates a unique key with a value. Knowing the key gives the app a direct lookup.

steps.label: Save session
steps.caption: The service stores the visitor's session details under k42.

steps.label: Present k42
steps.caption: The browser sends the session ID with its next request.

steps.label: Fetch k42
steps.caption: The store returns the matching value without searching other visitors. Finding sessions by city would need a different lookup.

story.technology: Redis can hold session records under keys and expire them after a chosen lifetime.

title: Document Store
lesson: A document store groups nested fields into records that can have different shapes. Embed data read and updated together, and check limits on document size and write contention.
example: A recipe includes its ingredients and steps in one document. An ever-growing list of reviews belongs elsewhere to keep the recipe manageable.
question: Which data is a good candidate to embed in a recipe document?
answers: Its bounded list of preparation steps
Every review it will ever receive
All recipes written by the same cook
why: The steps are small, bounded, and typically read with their recipe.
detail: Choose the document boundary around a unit of access. A single-document update can atomically change a recipe's ingredient quantities and serving count in engines offering document atomicity. Embedding a chef's whole profile in every recipe would duplicate frequent edits. A reference lets those recipes share one profile, at the cost of another lookup or a join-like operation when reading.

terms.definition: Storing related data inside the same document.
A field containing another record's identifier instead of a copy of its contents.

story.intro: A recipe screen always shows the ingredient list with the instructions. It would be handy to load them together.
story.meaning: A document store keeps related values, including lists and nested fields, in one record that an app can retrieve by ID.

steps.label: Save recipe
steps.caption: The editor places the curry's ingredients and steps inside one record.

steps.label: Read curry
steps.caption: One document read gives the screen what it needs to start cooking.

steps.label: Save separately
steps.caption: Reviews can grow for years. Storing them separately keeps the recipe itself small.

story.technology: MongoDB can embed a recipe's ingredient array and keep reviews in a separate collection.

title: Wide Column Store
lesson: Wide-column systems organize sparse data around row or partition keys and families of columns. In systems such as Cassandra, partition and clustering keys shape efficient reads within a partition.
example: A sensor log partitions by device and day, then orders readings by time. Looking up one device-hour is cheap, while a fleet-wide search needs a separate design.
question: A device's readings would grow forever under one partition key. Which change bounds it?
answers: Add a time bucket to the partition key
Store a longer device name
Reverse the sort order of timestamps
why: A new bucket creates a separate partition instead of extending one indefinitely.
detail: Design from an actual query such as “read this sensor's values between 10 and 11 yesterday.” A device-and-day key locates one partition. Within it, timestamp order permits a range read. A fleet-wide query for all low-battery devices cuts across those partitions. A second table keyed for battery alerts can make that query efficient, provided writes keep both representations current.

terms.definition: The fields used to locate the group of related rows on a storage node.
In systems such as Cassandra, fields defining the order of rows inside a partition.

story.intro: A gardener asks for sensor 8’s temperatures from lunchtime yesterday. There are millions of readings for the whole farm.
story.meaning: A wide-column store can arrange related readings together. In Cassandra, one key selects a group and another orders the rows within it.

steps.label: Choose device-day
steps.caption: Each reading carries a device ID and date. Together they identify a small group of readings.

steps.label: Order by time
steps.caption: The reading's timestamp determines its position within that group.

steps.label: Read lunchtime range
steps.caption: The chart selects sensor 8's day and a time range. A farm-wide search needs a different access plan.

story.technology: An Apache Cassandra table can use device and date as its partition key and time as its clustering column.

title: Graph Databases
lesson: A graph database models entities as vertices and relationships as edges. Traversals follow connections directly, but a search can still fan out sharply around highly connected vertices.
example: A mentoring app searches two hops from a learner for introductions. Limiting depth keeps the search fast and leaves out distant matches.
question: Which query benefits most directly from graph traversal?
answers: Find connections within two introductions of a mentor
Read a receipt by receipt ID
Fetch the latest temperature for a known sensor
why: The query depends on the structure of relationships over several steps.
detail: Estimate how many paths a query must explore. If each person has 100 contacts, following two hops can inspect roughly 10,000 links before removing duplicates. An index can locate the starting person, but traversal still pays for fan-out. Restrict edge types, stop at a chosen depth, or cap results when the application only needs a few introductions.

terms.definition: An entity in the graph, such as a person or a station.
A relationship connecting vertices, often carrying a direction, type, and properties.
The number of next steps a traversal or request generates.

story.intro: Lea wants a mentor someone she knows can introduce. A list of names alone does not reveal the introductions.
story.meaning: A graph database stores people or things and the relationships joining them. A search can follow those relationships one step at a time.

steps.label: Knows
steps.caption: The database follows a connection from Lea and finds Ari.

steps.label: Mentors with
steps.caption: A second relationship leads from Ari to Mei, a mentor.

steps.label: Return introduction
steps.caption: The app shows Lea the route through Ari. A limit of two steps keeps the search focused.

story.technology: Neo4j can match a path made of person nodes and named relationships.

title: NoSQL
lesson: NoSQL covers several nonrelational data models with different guarantees. Pick a model by the access path, then check the database's consistency settings and transaction limits.
example: A device service uses a key-value model for fast status lookups. Historical fleet analysis may need a second model optimized for scans.
question: A database is described only as NoSQL. What can you infer about transaction guarantees?
answers: They must be checked for that engine and configuration
All writes are eventually consistent
Multi-record transactions are always supported
why: The label describes a family of models, each with its own guarantees.
detail: BASE describes one approach to replicated data. Basically available means the design favors returning a response during disruption, possibly with stale data. Soft state means a replica's visible state can change as background updates arrive. Eventually consistent means replicas converge once writes stop and communication resumes under the system's assumptions. A regional follower count may temporarily show 98 instead of 100. A bank debit requiring a coordinated balance check needs stronger guarantees for that operation.

terms.definition: The system prioritizes useful service during partial failures, with possible degradation.
Background reconciliation can change visible values without another user write.
Replicas converge after updates cease and propagation and reconciliation can finish.

references.title: SQL vs. NoSQL Databases: What’s the Difference?

story.intro: An app stores activity counts for readers in two cities. One city sees 98 likes while the other already sees 100.
story.meaning: NoSQL is a family of databases using data shapes such as documents or key-value pairs. The chosen database and settings determine when readers see updates.

steps.label: Save new count
steps.caption: One region accepts a new count of 100 under the app's chosen update policy.

steps.label: Read local copy
steps.caption: This app allows an older local answer while the two regions exchange changes.

steps.label: Propagate changes
steps.caption: When updates finish traveling and writes settle, both copies agree. A payment balance may need stricter rules.

story.technology: Azure Cosmos DB offers several consistency levels, so the app explicitly chooses how fresh a regional read must be.

title: Caching
lesson: A cache keeps reusable data closer to the work that needs it. Decide what makes an entry fresh, how it expires, and what happens when many requests miss at once.
example: A menu cache cuts database traffic at lunch. A short expiry makes new prices visible sooner but increases misses.
question: The café updates the soup price to $9 in its database. Why might the menu still show $8?
answers: The cache still has a copy of the old price.
Each visitor gets a different database table.
A database always rounds prices down.
why: Updating the database does not automatically replace a cached value. Removing the old copy makes the next lookup fetch the new price.
detail: A 95% hit rate at 10,000 reads per second leaves the origin handling about 500 reads per second. If the cache restarts empty, the origin may suddenly receive all 10,000. Coalescing concurrent misses for the same key lets one request fetch while the others wait. Randomizing expiry times across keys can keep a whole batch from expiring together.

terms.definition: The fraction of lookups served by a usable cached entry.
A burst of overlapping rebuilds after entries become unavailable.
Removing an entry, often to free space before its normal expiry.

story.intro: Maya opens the café menu to check the price of soup. When Jo opens the same menu, does the app need to ask the database for the price again?
story.meaning: A cache is a place to keep a copy of data handy when you expect to need it again.

steps.label: Price?
steps.caption: The app asks the cache for the soup price. The cache has no copy yet, so this is a cache miss.

steps.label: Return $8
steps.caption: The app reads the original price from the database, where the café keeps its menu. The database sends back $8.

steps.label: Store $8
steps.caption: The app saves a copy of the $8 price and shows Maya the menu. The original stays in the database.

steps.label: Return $8
steps.caption: Jo opens the same menu and the cache returns $8. This cache hit lets the app skip the database lookup.

story.technology: The café could keep its menu in PostgreSQL and use Redis for the temporary copies.

title: Refresh Ahead
lesson: Refresh-ahead caching renews an entry before it expires. It can keep popular reads fast, but refreshing unused entries spends backend capacity unnecessarily.
example: Refresh tomorrow's train schedule just before its cache lifetime ends. Refresh only frequently used stations to avoid fetching schedules nobody requests.
question: A popular timetable briefly slows down every time its cache entry expires. Which change targets that pause?
answers: Rebuild the entry shortly before expiry
Shorten its expiry without changing refresh behavior
Drop the timetable after every successful read
why: Refreshing early can make the next value available before callers experience a miss.
detail: Choose when and what to refresh using both access frequency and rebuild time. If an entry takes two seconds to regenerate, starting one millisecond before expiry will still leave a gap. Let only one worker refresh a key at a time. If renewal fails, the product needs a policy for how long it may serve the previous value.

terms.definition: Time to live, the interval after which an entry expires under a cache's policy.
The period during which serving an older value is acceptable for this use.

story.intro: The ferry countdown freezes every time the timetable copy expires. Building a fresh copy takes two seconds.
story.meaning: Refresh ahead means fetching a replacement before a popular cached item expires, so the next reader can find it ready.

steps.label: Near expiry
steps.caption: The busy pier's timetable has five seconds left. A background job starts preparing a replacement.

steps.label: Fetch times
steps.caption: The worker asks for the latest times while riders still use the current copy.

steps.label: Replace copy
steps.caption: Two seconds later the new timetable is ready. The next rider can read it immediately.

story.technology: A scheduled worker can check popular Redis entries and replace their values shortly before expiry.

title: Write-behind
lesson: A write-behind cache accepts a write and persists it to the backing store later. Batching can improve throughput, but durability depends on what survives before the batch reaches storage.
example: A game buffers noncritical counter updates for a second. A crash can lose unflushed increments unless the buffer is durably logged.
question: A write was acknowledged, then the only in-memory buffer crashed before flushing. What is at risk?
answers: Loss of the acknowledged update
A read-only database becoming writable
Every previous batch being rolled back
why: The backing store never received that update and the only copy was volatile.
detail: Consider successive values for the same record. A worker flushes revision 12, crashes before recording completion, then later replays revision 11. A backing store that accepts the older value can move backward. Durable buffering, per-key ordering or revision checks, and monitoring the age of the oldest unflushed write help distinguish a fast acknowledgment from a completed persistence operation.

terms.definition: Transfer pending updates to the backing store.
A cached value with changes that have yet to reach durable backing storage.

story.intro: A game counts applause after a concert. Saving every clap to slow storage makes the button feel sluggish.
story.meaning: Write-behind accepts a change into a fast buffer and writes it to the permanent store later. An accepted change needs protection until it reaches that store.

steps.label: Add one clap
steps.caption: The buffer accepts the clap and the game updates the visible count.

steps.label: Group claps
steps.caption: The game collects 50 changes so one batch can replace many small writes.

steps.label: Save counts
steps.caption: The worker saves the batch. If the only buffer had disappeared before this point, accepted claps could have vanished.

story.technology: A game can batch counter changes before writing to PostgreSQL and keep a durable log if those changes must survive a crash.

title: Write-through
lesson: Write-through sends updates through the cache to the backing store, waiting for the backing write before reporting success. This keeps the normal read path warm, while adding work to the write path.
example: Changing a product description updates the store and cached copy before completion. The caller now experiences the store's write latency.
question: The backing store is slow during a write-through update. What usually happens to the client's write?
answers: Acknowledgment takes longer
The write always succeeds immediately
The cache automatically switches to write-behind
why: Successful acknowledgment depends on completing the backing write.
detail: Walk through a partial failure. The backing store commits a new price, then the cache update fails. A retry should be safe, and an invalidation or repair step can prevent an old entry from continuing to win reads. Even synchronous write-through needs a stated policy for such failures. Writers that bypass the cache can also create stale entries.

terms.definition: The sequence of operations required to accept a change.
Marking a cached copy unusable so a future read obtains current data.

story.intro: The bakery changes the name of a cake. The next visitor should see the new name from the fast copy.
story.meaning: Write-through handles a change through the cache and waits for the backing store before it reports success.

steps.label: Rename cake
steps.caption: The editor sends the new name through the cache's write path.

steps.label: Persist name
steps.caption: The write waits for the menu database to confirm the new name. Slow storage makes the editor wait too.

steps.label: Confirm change
steps.caption: After the store and cached value have been updated successfully, the editor gets confirmation and later reads can use the copy.

story.technology: A write-through layer can coordinate writes to Redis and PostgreSQL and invalidate a copy if its update fails.

title: Cache Aside
lesson: The application reads the cache first. On a miss it reads the source and fills the cache. Updates need an invalidation or expiry policy to limit old values.
example: A library caches book details by ISBN. Evicting a changed entry forces the next request to rebuild it, adding latency to that read.
question: In cache-aside, who fetches a missing record and fills the cache?
answers: The application handling the read
A mandatory background writer
The database transaction log alone
why: Cache-aside puts the miss and refill logic in the application.
detail: A subtle race occurs when a reader misses and loads the old value, a writer updates storage and evicts the key, then the reader inserts its old value. The cache now appears freshly populated with stale data. A short expiry limits exposure. If immediate correctness matters, guard updates with versions or perform that particular read against authoritative storage.

terms.definition: A lookup with no usable value under the requested key.
A comparison that prevents an older revision from replacing a newer one.

story.intro: A library app checks its shelf of recent book descriptions. Nobody has opened this book yet.
story.meaning: In cache-aside, the application decides what to do on a miss. It fetches the original and fills the cache itself.

steps.label: Look up ISBN
steps.caption: There is no description under this ISBN, so the application takes over.

steps.label: Send description
steps.caption: The app fetches the authoritative description for that book.

steps.label: Fill cache
steps.caption: The app saves the result under the ISBN. After an edit, it can evict that copy so the next reader fetches the new text.

story.technology: A library service can implement cache-aside with Redis for copies and PostgreSQL for book records.

title: Client Caching
lesson: A client cache keeps a reusable response on the user's device. HTTP freshness rules can avoid a request, and a validator such as an ETag can check whether a stored response still applies.
example: A versioned illustration stays in the browser cache across visits. Shipping a new version under a new filename prevents browsers from reusing the old illustration.
question: Which design permits a long freshness lifetime for a logo while still shipping updates promptly?
answers: Use a new content-hashed URL when the logo changes
Reuse one URL and never revalidate it
Place the logo in each HTML response
why: A changed file gets a distinct cache key, so the old fresh entry cannot hide the update.
detail: Freshness and validation save different costs. A still-fresh cached response can be reused without contacting the origin. After it becomes stale, the browser can send its ETag in an If-None-Match request. If the representation is unchanged, a 304 response saves the body transfer but still costs a round trip. Personalized responses also need a policy that controls shared storage.

terms.definition: An opaque validator identifying a version of a representation.
An HTTP response telling the client its conditional request can reuse a previously stored representation.

story.intro: Alex opens a museum guide twice. Should the phone download the same floor map on both visits?
story.meaning: Client caching lets a browser store a response on the visitor's device and reuse it according to the server's rules.

steps.label: Send floor map
steps.caption: The map has a versioned filename and permission to reuse the response for a day.

steps.label: Keep map
steps.caption: The phone saves the response under that map's URL.

steps.label: Read local map
steps.caption: An hour later the URL still matches and the copy is fresh. The phone can show it without another map request.

story.technology: A web server can send a Cache-Control max-age with a hashed asset filename that changes when the map changes.

title: CDN Caching
lesson: A content delivery network stores reusable responses at edge locations near users. Its cache key and sharing rules must account for inputs that change the response.
example: An edge serves public album covers quickly worldwide. Personalized account pages need separate handling to avoid sharing private content.
question: A CDN keys pages only by URL, but the account page depends on a login cookie. What should the team do first?
answers: Keep personalized pages out of the shared cache
Increase the cache lifetime
Add more edge locations
why: The same URL can return private data for different people, so sharing its cached response is unsafe.
detail: Two clients request the same article in different languages. If the origin selects language from a header, the edge must distinguish that header when caching variants. Vary or an explicit CDN cache-key configuration can express this. Adding every incoming header instead would create many near-duplicate entries and reduce hits. Include only inputs that actually affect the shareable response.

terms.definition: An HTTP response header identifying request headers used to select a representation.
A network site near clients that can answer requests from a CDN cache.

story.intro: Fans in Sydney keep opening an album cover stored across the ocean. The same image makes the long trip again and again.
story.meaning: A content delivery network, or CDN, can cache a shared file at an edge location close to visitors.

steps.label: Request cover
steps.caption: The nearby edge checks for a reusable copy of the public cover.

steps.label: Send cover
steps.caption: On the first miss, the edge fetches the image from the original server and keeps a copy.

steps.label: Serve saved cover
steps.caption: The next fan gets the cover from the nearby edge while the copy remains fresh.

story.technology: CloudFront can serve an album cover from an edge cache while Amazon S3 holds the original object.

title: Web Server Caching
lesson: A web server or reverse proxy can keep generated pages or fragments near the application origin. A hit skips rendering work even when the user has never visited before.
example: A local proxy caches a concert lineup for thirty seconds. A lineup correction may take that long to appear without a purge.
question: Two visitors hit the same origin and only the first request runs the page renderer. Which layer can explain this?
answers: A shared web server response cache
A private browser history entry
A database disk buffer alone
why: A shared response cache can answer the second request before it reaches rendering.
detail: Caching a full HTML response skips routing, queries, and rendering on a hit, but every visitor must be allowed to see the same page. If a header includes an unread-message count, cache the public lineup fragment and render the personal header per request. A new ticket price may then invalidate one fragment without rebuilding every possible personalized page.

terms.definition: Storage for reusable pieces of a rendered page.
A server in front of origin services that can route requests and sometimes cache responses.

story.intro: Every visitor asks for the same festival lineup, and the web app builds the same HTML each time.
story.meaning: A web server or a server in front of it can cache the finished response and serve it to later visitors.

steps.label: Request lineup
steps.caption: The proxy checks for an already-rendered lineup. Its cache is empty.

steps.label: Return HTML
steps.caption: The app renders the public lineup once. The proxy saves the response for a short time.

steps.label: Serve saved HTML
steps.caption: The next request arrives before expiry, so the web app skips rebuilding the page.

story.technology: NGINX can use its proxy cache for a public lineup page while passing personal account requests to the app.

title: Database Caching
lesson: Database engines retain frequently read data and index pages in memory to reduce storage I/O. A warm buffer cache can help repeated reads even when the SQL still runs each time.
example: A book index fits in the buffer pool after the first scan. Reads avoid disk access, though filtering and sorting still consume CPU.
question: The same query executes twice and the second run reads fewer pages from disk. What is a likely reason?
answers: Needed pages stayed in the database buffer cache
The database disabled all transaction checks
The second query skipped all CPU work
why: Cached pages avoid repeated storage reads while query execution continues.
detail: Distinguish a page cache from a result cache. A warm database buffer pool supplies table and index pages from memory, yet a query can still join and aggregate them repeatedly. A result cache stores the final answer and must know when underlying data has changed. Compare physical reads, query CPU, and repeat frequency before deciding which layer will save work.

terms.definition: Memory reserved by the database engine for frequently accessed storage pages.
Storage for a query's computed output so a repeat request can skip computation.

story.intro: Looking up a word in a giant dictionary is slower the first time than the second. The query text stays exactly the same.
story.meaning: A database can keep recently used chunks of stored data in memory so later queries avoid another disk read.

steps.label: Need index page
steps.caption: The engine looks for a small chunk of the dictionary index. That chunk is absent from memory.

steps.label: Load page
steps.caption: It reads the page from storage and keeps a copy in the database's memory.

steps.label: Reuse page
steps.caption: The engine still runs the query, but the needed page is already in memory.

story.technology: PostgreSQL uses shared buffers to hold database pages, and its query plan can report buffer hits and reads.

title: Application Caching
lesson: Application code can cache a computed value or domain object using a key that reflects its inputs. Process-local caches are fast, while a shared cache helps many instances reuse the same result.
example: An offer service caches shipping quotes by origin, destination, weight, and carrier. Omitting weight makes a cheaper quote leak into a heavier parcel's estimate.
question: A cached quote for a light parcel appears on a heavier parcel. Which fix addresses the cause?
answers: Include weight in the quote's cache key
Increase the cache capacity
Cache the same key on more service instances
why: The key must distinguish every input that can change the result.
detail: Simulate an edit with three application instances. Clearing an in-process entry on server A leaves copies on B and C unchanged. A distributed invalidation message can clear those copies, but a disconnected instance may miss it. A bounded TTL limits that case. A shared cache simplifies visibility across instances while adding network latency and another component to operate.

terms.definition: A cache accessible only inside one running application process.
The identifier combining the inputs that determine which stored result may be reused.

story.intro: A parcel shop asks for the same shipping quote many times. How can it reuse the answer without mixing up heavy and light parcels?
story.meaning: Application caching saves a value the app computed under a key that represents the inputs that affect it.

steps.label: Enter details
steps.caption: The parcel weighs 2 kg and travels from Sydney to Perth with a chosen carrier.

steps.label: Save priced route
steps.caption: After getting the price, the app keys the result by route, carrier and weight.

steps.label: Match inputs
steps.caption: A matching parcel can reuse the quote. A 5 kg parcel needs a different key.

story.technology: A shipping service can share Redis quote entries across application instances and expire them when rates change.

title: Asynchronism
lesson: Asynchronous work lets the caller continue before the job finishes. Design separate signals for acceptance, completion, and failure so users can tell what happened.
example: A photo app accepts an upload and queues thumbnail creation. Browsing stays responsive, with a placeholder until processing finishes.
question: An import API replies that a job was accepted. Which claim can it safely make?
answers: The system accepted the work for processing
Every row has been imported successfully
The resulting file is already available
why: Acceptance and completion are distinct states in an asynchronous flow.
detail: Allocate a durable job identifier before telling the user their upload was accepted. Record transitions such as queued, running, succeeded, and failed so the UI can reconnect to the job. A background crash can leave a job looking active forever. A lease, heartbeat, or reconciliation process lets the system find abandoned work and decide whether it is safe to retry.

terms.definition: A durable description of where work is in its lifecycle.
A time-limited claim granting a worker the right to perform a task.

story.intro: Tara uploads a photo on a bus. Making six thumbnails takes longer than saving the photo.
story.meaning: Asynchronous work lets the caller move on while another part of the system finishes a job. The app must show which part has actually finished.

steps.label: Accept upload
steps.caption: The app saves the photo and a durable job ID. Tara sees a pending thumbnail.

steps.label: Build thumbnails
steps.caption: A background worker builds the six sizes while Tara continues browsing.

steps.label: Mark ready
steps.caption: The app can now show the thumbnail. A failed job would need a separate status.

story.technology: An HTTP upload endpoint can return 202 Accepted and a status URL that the photo app can check.

title: Back Pressure
lesson: Back pressure tells producers to slow down when consumers cannot keep up. Bounded queues, demand signals, and admission limits keep excess work from exhausting memory.
example: A video processor stops requesting new frames while its buffer is full. Playback may pause, but the buffer stays within its memory budget.
question: A consumer consistently handles 80 jobs per second while 100 arrive. Which option prevents unbounded growth?
answers: Limit admitted work to sustainable capacity
Double the queue size once
Acknowledge jobs before doing them
why: A larger buffer only delays saturation while the arrival rate exceeds the drain rate.
detail: If 100 jobs arrive each second and workers finish 80, backlog grows by 20 per second. A buffer with 1,000 empty slots will fill in about 50 seconds at that rate. Decide where the next arrival should wait, be rejected, or be dropped. Communicating that decision to producers helps them reduce demand before memory is exhausted.

terms.definition: A queue with an explicit maximum capacity.
Rejecting or discarding lower-priority work to protect capacity for the rest.

story.intro: A video player receives frames faster than it can display them. Its memory is filling up.
story.meaning: Back pressure is a signal from a busy receiver telling the sender to slow down or pause.

steps.label: Send frames
steps.caption: The producer fills the buffer faster than the player can drain it.

steps.label: Pause intake
steps.caption: The receiver signals that there is no space for more frames. The producer pauses.

steps.label: Request more
steps.caption: Playback frees space, so the receiver asks for another small batch.

story.technology: Node.js streams expose back pressure when a write returns false and signal when writing can resume with a drain event.

title: Task Queues
lesson: A task queue holds units of work for workers to execute outside the request path. Retries help recover from interrupted work, so handlers should tolerate repeated execution.
example: A worker generates a PDF and stores it under the report ID. Reusing that ID avoids producing extra files if delivery repeats.
question: A worker dies after saving a PDF but before acknowledging the task. What should its replacement expect?
answers: It may receive and execute the same task again
The broker can infer that the PDF was saved
The original task can never be redelivered
why: The broker may retry unacknowledged work even though its external effect already happened.
detail: Set a visibility timeout long enough for typical work and renew it for valid long-running jobs. If it expires while a worker is still processing, a second worker may start the task. Repeated failure on one malformed job can waste the entire pool. Cap retries, record the terminal error, and transfer that job to a holding queue for inspection.

terms.definition: An interval that hides a claimed message from other workers before acknowledgment.
A separate destination for messages the normal consumer repeatedly fails to process.

story.intro: Eva requests a large PDF. She wants to close the tab without losing the job.
story.meaning: A task queue holds work instructions until a worker can carry them out and confirm completion.

steps.label: Enqueue report 51
steps.caption: The app saves a task with report ID 51 before telling Eva it was accepted.

steps.label: Deliver report task
steps.caption: An available worker takes the task and creates the PDF under that report ID.

steps.label: Acknowledge completion
steps.caption: The worker confirms after saving the file. Using the same report ID helps if an interrupted attempt is delivered again.

story.technology: A Celery worker can consume queued PDF-generation tasks and save results under stable report IDs.

title: Message Queues
lesson: A queue buffers messages between senders and receivers with independent lifetimes. Delivery, ordering, retention, and acknowledgment guarantees vary by broker and configuration.
example: Checkout places a receipt request on a durable queue while email workers are offline. Messages wait within retention limits, increasing delivery latency.
question: Email workers stop briefly while checkout stays healthy. Which capability lets requests wait for recovery?
answers: Durable buffering with sufficient retention
A synchronous call with no timeout
Immediate deletion on producer acknowledgment
why: A retained message survives the consumer outage and can be processed after recovery.
detail: If several workers share one queue, a message normally goes to one worker for a given delivery attempt. If billing and analytics must each see every new order, give each a subscription or queue fed by the same event. Track the oldest message age as well as depth. Ten old payment messages can matter more than 100 fresh analytics events.

terms.definition: A consumer's signal that the broker may consider a delivery handled.
The time or conditions under which the broker keeps a message available.

story.intro: Email delivery is paused for maintenance. Customers can still place orders if their receipt requests have somewhere to wait.
story.meaning: A message queue holds messages until a receiver is ready, letting senders and receivers work at different times.

steps.label: Send receipt request
steps.caption: Checkout records a message with the order ID in a queue configured to retain it.

steps.label: Wait for worker
steps.caption: While email is offline, retained receipt requests accumulate.

steps.label: Deliver waiting request
steps.caption: The worker resumes, sends the receipt, and acknowledges processing. It should recognize a duplicate if delivery repeats.

story.technology: Amazon SQS can keep receipt messages for a configured retention period until consumers process them.

title: Idempotent Operations
lesson: An idempotent operation has the same intended effect when repeated with the same input. A stable request key and an atomic record of the result can protect business actions from duplicate retries.
example: A checkout retries a payment after a timeout using the original idempotency key. Keeping the key and result costs storage but avoids a second charge.
question: A client times out after submitting a payment. Which retry design prevents a duplicate charge?
answers: Reuse a key the server atomically associates with that payment
Generate a new key for each attempt
Wait ten seconds and send the original charge as a new request
why: A stable key lets the server recognize the earlier operation even if its response was lost.
detail: Scope the key to the caller and operation, and record a fingerprint of the request. A retry carrying the same payment key and amount can receive the earlier result. Reusing that key with a different amount should produce a conflict. Determine how long to retain keys from the client's retry window. An expired key can make a late retry look new.

terms.definition: A stable client-supplied identifier for one intended operation across retries.
A representation of the relevant payload used to detect conflicting reuse of a key.

story.intro: A payment succeeds, but the reply disappears. Tapping pay again should not charge Ana twice.
story.meaning: An idempotent operation has the same intended effect when repeated. A payment service can remember a stable request ID and its result.

steps.label: Pay with key A
steps.caption: The app creates one key for Ana's intended payment.

steps.label: Record charge result
steps.caption: The service associates the key with the charge and its result. The reply to the phone is lost.

steps.label: Retry key A
steps.caption: The service recognizes the matching request and returns the recorded result without another charge.

story.technology: Stripe's API accepts an idempotency key on payment-related POST requests so a caller can safely retry the same intent.

title: Communication
lesson: A service boundary requires a protocol, a message format, and a failure policy. A missing reply leaves the caller uncertain whether the remote action ran.
example: A ticket service times out contacting inventory. Asking inventory about the original reservation ID adds a lookup but avoids a blind second reservation.
question: A request times out before its reply arrives. What can the caller conclude?
answers: The outcome is uncertain without further evidence
The server definitely rejected the request
The server definitely completed the request
why: Either the request or the response may have been delayed or lost.
detail: Draw both the request and the return route. If the inventory service commits a reservation and its response is lost, a successful connection alone cannot tell the caller what happened. Agree on an operation ID, an outcome lookup, and what a timeout means. Decide which fields can evolve independently so a rolling deployment can still exchange understandable messages.

terms.definition: The rules for how peers structure messages and interpret their exchange.
Encoding an in-memory value into bytes that another process can decode.

references.title: Everything you need to know about HTTP

story.intro: A ticket app asks another server to hold seat 4. The connection breaks before the reply arrives.
story.meaning: Communication between services needs an agreed message format and rules for handling a missing answer.

steps.label: Hold seat 4
steps.caption: The request includes reservation ID R6 so the two services can refer to the same action.

steps.label: Record hold
steps.caption: The seat is held, but the reply disappears on the way back.

steps.label: Check R6
steps.caption: The caller asks about R6 and learns that the hold succeeded, avoiding a second reservation.

story.technology: An HTTP API can expose a reservation status URL keyed by the original reservation ID.

title: HTTP
lesson: HTTP describes requests and responses using methods, targets, headers, status codes, and optional bodies. Method semantics let clients and intermediaries reason about safety, retries, and caching.
example: A reader fetches a chapter with GET. A crawler may issue that request too, so changing a subscription as a side effect would be unsafe.
question: Which action belongs behind GET?
answers: Retrieve the current reading list
Cancel a reader's subscription
Submit a purchase using the current cart
why: Clients reasonably expect a GET to retrieve a representation without requesting a state change.
detail: Use the method and status code together to describe progress. Creating a report immediately can return 201 with its location. Accepting a report request for later processing can return 202 and a status URL. A client that receives 202 should display pending work and check the status resource. A successful HTTP exchange does not by itself mean the report exists.

terms.definition: The bytes and metadata conveying a resource's state in a chosen format.
An HTTP method whose requested semantics are read-only, such as GET or HEAD.

references.title: Everything you need to know about HTTP

story.intro: A weather app needs today’s forecast. How does it ask the server a question the server understands?
story.meaning: HTTP defines request methods, addresses, headers and responses so clients and servers can exchange information.

steps.label: GET forecast
steps.caption: The app sends GET for a URL identifying Sydney's forecast, asking to read it.

steps.label: Return 200
steps.caption: A 200 status says the request succeeded, and the response body carries the temperatures.

steps.label: Show forecast
steps.caption: The app reads the returned values and displays them. A missing location would need a different response.

story.technology: The browser's fetch API can issue a GET and expose the HTTP status and JSON response.

title: TCP
lesson: TCP provides a reliable, ordered stream of bytes over a connection. It preserves byte order but leaves message boundaries to the application protocol.
example: A chat protocol prefixes each frame with its length. This adds a little overhead and allows a reader to recover frames from arbitrary receive chunks.
question: A single TCP read returns half of a chat message. What should the receiver do?
answers: Buffer bytes until the protocol's complete frame arrives
Assume the sender truncated the message
Treat every TCP read as a complete application record
why: TCP can split or combine application writes while preserving the byte stream.
detail: In an ordered stream, a missing segment can hold up delivery of later bytes to the application until retransmission succeeds. A successful local write only shows that the operating system accepted bytes for sending. Even acknowledgment by the remote TCP stack does not prove the application committed a purchase. A business-level response or outcome lookup must carry that information.

terms.definition: An application convention for finding individual messages within a byte stream.
Later work must wait for an earlier missing or unfinished item.

story.intro: Chat sends the word HELLO. The receiver's first read contains only HE.
story.meaning: TCP delivers an ordered stream of bytes. The receiving app needs its own rule for telling where one message ends.

steps.label: Prefix length 5
steps.caption: The chat protocol puts the message length before the five letters.

steps.label: Deliver HE
steps.caption: The receiver sees that two letters are too few. It keeps the partial message.

steps.label: Deliver LLO
steps.caption: Five letters have now arrived in order, so the receiver can show HELLO.

story.technology: A Node.js TCP socket can buffer incoming chunks until its application protocol has a complete message.

title: UDP
lesson: UDP sends independent datagrams without built-in delivery, ordering, or retransmission guarantees. Applications decide how to handle missing or late packets and how to control their sending rate.
example: A voice call skips a late audio frame to keep speech timely. Occasional gaps are preferable to waiting on outdated audio.
question: A live voice packet arrives after its playback deadline. What policy often suits this workload?
answers: Discard it and continue with timely audio
Pause the call until all earlier packets arrive
Assume UDP will reorder it before delivery
why: Past its deadline the packet has little value, while waiting increases conversational delay.
detail: Imagine a game server sends player positions 41, 42, and 43. When 43 arrives before 42, an application-level sequence number can let the client discard the older update. A purchase made inside that game needs different delivery semantics and may use a reliable stream. UDP still needs congestion control at the protocol or application layer for sustained traffic.

terms.definition: A single message delivered as one unit if it arrives.
An application or protocol counter used to recognize newer, duplicate, or missing messages.

story.intro: During a voice call, one sound packet arrives after the conversation has already moved on.
story.meaning: UDP sends separate packets called datagrams. The network can lose or reorder them, so the app decides what to do.

steps.label: Send audio 8
steps.caption: The caller labels a short piece of sound with a number. Packet 8 is delayed.

steps.label: Deliver audio 9
steps.caption: The player receives the next piece first and uses its timing information for playback.

steps.label: Miss deadline
steps.caption: The deadline for packet 8 passes. Skipping the late sound keeps the call from falling further behind.

story.technology: A real-time audio protocol such as RTP can carry sequence numbers and timestamps over UDP.

title: RPC
lesson: Remote procedure call exposes an operation on another process through a method-like interface. A call still crosses a network, so deadlines, partial failure, and serialization matter.
example: A recommendation service calls a ranking method with a forty-millisecond deadline. A fallback list keeps the page usable if ranking runs late.
question: Why give a remote method call a deadline?
answers: To bound the time the caller spends waiting
To prove the remote operation never started
To guarantee the reply will arrive in order
why: A deadline protects the caller's time budget even when the server or network is slow.
detail: A web endpoint has a 300 ms budget and spends 180 ms before calling search. Giving search a fresh 300 ms timeout can exceed the user's deadline. Pass the remaining budget downstream and include time for assembling the reply. If the caller cancels, the remote handler must cooperate to stop unnecessary work. A timeout alone cannot undo an action already committed.

terms.definition: Passing the caller's remaining time budget through nested calls.
Generated or handwritten client code that encodes a method call and handles its response.
An interaction model in which a client invokes a named procedure in another process.

story.intro: A shop screen calls getDeliveryDate as though it were a nearby function. The delivery service lives on another machine.
story.meaning: A remote procedure call, or RPC, sends a named operation and its inputs to another process and receives a result or error.

steps.label: Call delivery method
steps.caption: The client packages the destination and item ID into a request.

steps.label: Send request
steps.caption: The service receives the message and computes the date. The call now depends on the network as well as code.

steps.label: Return date
steps.caption: The screen displays the result if it arrives before its deadline, or shows an estimate-unavailable state.

story.technology: A gRPC client stub can expose a delivery method and set a deadline on its remote call.

title: REST
lesson: REST models a system as resources with representations and a uniform interface. Requests carry the context needed to process them, and HTTP methods express common operations on resources.
example: A library exposes a loan at /loans/42. Different clients can retrieve the same resource through a stable URL, though complex workflows may need several interactions.
question: Which interface best reflects a resource-oriented design for retrieving one loan?
answers: GET /loans/42
POST /executeGetLoan with an action parameter
PUT /loans/42 with an empty body
why: The URI identifies the loan and the HTTP method describes retrieval.
detail: Expose the state of a long-running export through a resource. POST to a collection creates an export request, and a Location header can point to its URL. A client can later GET that URL to see progress or retrieve a result link. Keep permissions on each request and use validators when concurrent editors must avoid overwriting newer representations.

terms.definition: An identifiable concept, such as one export job, that a client may address through a URI.
A request carrying enough context for processing without relying on an earlier conversational step stored on one server.
An architectural style in which clients manipulate resources through representations and a uniform interface.

references.title: Visit the Dedicated API Design Roadmap

story.intro: The library wants a stable address for each book loan. Different clients should be able to read the same loan.
story.meaning: REST organizes an interface around identifiable resources. The request describes an action on a resource using agreed operations such as HTTP GET.

steps.label: Request loan 42
steps.caption: GET /loans/42 identifies one loan and asks to retrieve its current representation.

steps.label: Return due date
steps.caption: The response describes the loan, including which book it covers and when it is due.

steps.label: GET again
steps.caption: Using the same URL retrieves the current representation after a librarian extends the loan.

story.technology: A web API can return JSON at GET /loans/42 and check the reader's permission on each request.

title: gRPC
lesson: gRPC defines services and methods with a shared contract, commonly using Protocol Buffers. Generated clients support typed calls and streaming, while schema compatibility matters as services evolve.
example: A telemetry service streams sensor batches over one call. Adding a new field can be compatible, while reusing a retired field number can corrupt interpretation.
question: A team removes a Protocol Buffers field. How should it handle the old field number?
answers: Reserve it so future fields cannot reuse it
Immediately assign it to the next unrelated field
Renumber all following fields to fill the gap
why: Field numbers identify data on the wire, so reuse can mislead older clients.
detail: Choose a unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, or bidirectional method according to who must send multiple messages. A stream delivering thousands of readings still needs bounded buffering when the receiver slows down. For a rolling deployment, add new fields with fresh numbers and compatible defaults. Exercise old clients against new servers since business assumptions can break even when decoding succeeds.

terms.definition: A schema language and binary encoding using numbered fields.
A method invocation with one request message and one response message.
An RPC framework that uses a service contract to generate clients and servers and supports unary and streaming calls.

story.intro: A dashboard needs a stream of readings from a sensor service. Both teams need to agree on what a reading contains.
story.meaning: gRPC lets services define named calls and typed messages in a shared contract, often a Protocol Buffers file.

steps.label: Define reading
steps.caption: The contract names the method and assigns field numbers to device ID and temperature. Tools generate client code from it.

steps.label: Subscribe to sensor
steps.caption: The client starts a streaming method for sensor 8.

steps.label: Stream readings
steps.caption: The server can send multiple readings on the same call. New fields need fresh numbers so older clients can still decode messages.

story.technology: A .proto service definition can declare a server-streaming gRPC method returning a sequence of Reading messages.

title: GraphQL
lesson: GraphQL lets a client select fields from a typed schema in a single operation. Resolvers fetch those fields, so nested selections may still trigger a large amount of backend work.
example: A mobile screen requests titles and cover URLs without fetching reviews. A resolver that loads each cover separately can still generate many database calls.
question: One GraphQL request lists 100 books and makes 100 separate author lookups. What targets this cost?
answers: Batch author lookups by ID within the request
Force clients to request more book fields
Rename the author field in the schema
why: Batching addresses repeated backend calls that a single client request can hide.
detail: Work through a feed operation with twenty items, each selecting an author. A naive resolver issues twenty reads, even if only three authors occur. Collect keys during the request, fetch the three authors in a batch, then map results back in the requested order. Keep batch caches scoped appropriately so results authorized for one user cannot leak to another.

terms.definition: Code that supplies a value for a field in a GraphQL operation.
One initial lookup followed by an additional lookup for each result.
A typed query language and execution model in which a client selects the fields it wants from a schema.

story.intro: A phone bookshop needs a title and cover image. The desktop shop also wants an author biography.
story.meaning: GraphQL lets a client name the fields it needs from a schema, which is the API's description of available types and fields.

steps.label: Select two fields
steps.caption: The phone asks for title and cover URL for the book.

steps.label: Resolve requested fields
steps.caption: Functions called resolvers obtain the requested values. Nested fields may require extra reads.

steps.label: Return chosen fields
steps.caption: The result contains the requested fields. A desktop client can request a different selection from the same API.

story.technology: A GraphQL server can batch author lookups made by several book resolvers during one request.

title: Performance Antipatterns
lesson: A performance antipattern is a recurring design choice that creates avoidable work or contention. Identify the limiting resource under realistic load before changing the architecture.
example: A checkout slows during a sale. Traces show connection-pool wait time dominates, so adding API replicas alone could increase pressure on the same database.
question: A system becomes slow at peak load. What gives the most useful first evidence?
answers: A representative trace and resource metrics during the slowdown
The average response time from an idle development machine
The programming language's best benchmark score
why: Measurements from the failing workload reveal where time and capacity actually go.
detail: Test the smallest hypothesis that explains the observed slowdown. If response time grows as traffic rises while CPU stays flat, inspect waiting time for connections, locks, or downstream services. Change one suspected constraint and repeat the same workload. If throughput barely moves, the earlier symptom may have been a consequence of a different bottleneck.

terms.definition: The resource or stage currently limiting end-to-end capacity.
Work waiting because available capacity is occupied.

story.intro: The lunch rush makes checkout slow. Adding another web server yesterday barely changed the wait.
story.meaning: A performance antipattern is a repeated design choice that creates unnecessary work or waiting under load.

steps.label: Measure wait
steps.caption: A trace breaks one checkout into timed steps. Most time is spent waiting for a database connection.

steps.label: Count open connections
steps.caption: The pool is full of idle clients that each request opened and kept. The database has no spare slots.

steps.label: Reuse clients
steps.caption: The team tests a shared connection pool under the same demand and checks whether the wait shrinks.

story.technology: An OpenTelemetry trace and a database connection-pool metric can reveal where a slow request really waits.

title: Busy Database
lesson: A database becomes a bottleneck when it spends scarce capacity on work that could run elsewhere. Keep filtering and set-oriented operations near data, and move unrelated computation to suitable workers.
example: A transaction database renders invoice PDFs. Moving rendering to workers frees database CPU but adds a job handoff.
question: Which task is the clearest candidate to move off a saturated transaction database?
answers: Formatting invoice graphics into PDFs
Filtering rows by an indexed customer key
Checking a foreign key during an insert
why: PDF rendering consumes compute without benefiting from the engine's access to relational data.
detail: Break down what database time actually buys. Sorting a small filtered set near its data may save a large transfer, while building a printable PDF spends database CPU on presentation. Capture execution time, rows sent, and peak resource demand before moving work. Extracting too much logic can simply replace a CPU bottleneck with millions of row transfers.

terms.definition: Executing filtering or aggregation close to stored data to reduce data movement.
Multiple operations competing for the same limited resource.

story.intro: The orders database is busy drawing invoice PDFs. Meanwhile, simple purchases queue behind it.
story.meaning: A busy database antipattern occurs when work that belongs elsewhere consumes resources needed to store and query data.

steps.label: Run renderer
steps.caption: The database spends processor time arranging fonts and graphics while checkouts wait.

steps.label: Return invoice rows
steps.caption: The app changes the flow so the database returns just the invoice data.

steps.label: Render invoice
steps.caption: A separate worker draws the document. The database can use more of its time for orders.

story.technology: A PostgreSQL query can supply invoice rows to a PDF-generation worker running outside the database.

title: Busy Frontend
lesson: Request-serving processes have limited CPU and memory. Heavy background work in those same processes can starve interactive requests even after the original request returns.
example: An API starts video encodes in local background threads. Moving them to separately scaled workers protects page latency at the cost of queueing jobs.
question: Pages slow down whenever video encoding starts inside the API process. Which change provides resource isolation?
answers: Run encoders in a separate worker pool
Launch more encoding threads in the API process
Return the upload response earlier while encoding stays in the same process
why: Separate capacity keeps CPU-hungry background work from consuming the web tier's resources.
detail: A request can return quickly and still leave trouble behind. Starting an image resize on a local background thread frees the request handler but consumes the same machine's CPU and memory. Compare page latency with worker concurrency while applying a fixed upload load. Moving work to a separately bounded pool lets you set different capacity and failure limits for each tier.

terms.definition: A bounded group of executors serving a class of background jobs.
Limiting how much one workload can consume from another workload's capacity.

story.intro: One upload starts an expensive video resize. Suddenly other visitors' pages take ages to open.
story.meaning: A busy frontend happens when heavy work uses the same resources as the process that serves interactive requests.

steps.label: Start resize
steps.caption: The web process uses its processor for the resize and has less capacity for page requests.

steps.label: Queue resize
steps.caption: The app records the job and can send the uploader a pending response.

steps.label: Process video
steps.caption: A separately sized worker builds the file while the web process continues serving visitors.

story.technology: A web app can use a separate worker process to run FFmpeg instead of running encodes inside its request-serving process.

title: Chatty I/O
lesson: Many tiny calls can spend more time on round trips than on useful work. Batching or fetching related records together reduces trips, provided the batch stays reasonably sized.
example: A bookshelf sends one query per book to load its author. One batched query cuts latency but needs a limit for very large shelves.
question: A page runs fifty one-millisecond queries in sequence across a ten-millisecond network. What should improve latency most directly?
answers: Batch the related lookups into fewer round trips
Compress the text of each tiny query
Increase the length of each query timeout
